name: Mandibular distraction osteogenesis

angle.text: A bone-stretching technique that lengthens the lower jaw gradually, discussed in hardmaxxing circles for a longer, more projected jaw. The lengthening is visible in profile. It is well documented in children with congenital conditions and unstudied for purely cosmetic use.

summary: Gradual lower-jaw lengthening with a bone-stretching device, well documented in children with congenital conditions, unstudied for purely cosmetic use.
note: Evidence is from congenital and airway cases; nerve injury and infection are documented complications.
currentQuick:
Mandibular distraction cuts the lower jaw and slowly stretches the gap with a device so new bone forms. It is established for children with small jaws and airway obstruction, such as Pierre Robin sequence.
The literature is mainly case series and cohort reports; no studies of cosmetic use in people without a deformity were found.
How it works: After a cut and a week-long latency, the device lengthens the jaw at about 1 mm per day, followed by a consolidation period as bone matures. Devices can be external or internal.
Risks and caveats: A large review of 3,278 craniofacial cases documents complications; summaries report infection, hardware failure, and inferior alveolar nerve, tooth bud or facial nerve injury in a minority of cases.
deepLead:
Mandibular distraction osteogenesis (MDO) is a surgical technique that lengthens the lower jaw gradually. The bone is cut and the segments are slowly separated by a device, so new bone forms in the gap. The principle derives from Ilizarov's work on long bones, who showed bone forms when stretched along its axis at about 1 mm per day.
The modern clinical era in the jaw is dated to 1992 reports of gradual mandibular lengthening by McCarthy and colleagues. A 1995 report described an oblique corticotomy technique used in 87 patients. Its best-documented uses are in mandibular hypoplasia such as hemifacial microsomia and Treacher Collins syndrome, and in infants with micrognathia and airway obstruction, such as in Pierre Robin sequence.
Published evidence is mostly case series and cohort reports in children with congenital conditions. In looksmaxxing culture it is mentioned among procedures for adults seeking mandibular advancement; the sources reviewed describe no studies of cosmetic use in people without a deformity.

name: Total maxillary osteotomy

angle.text: Classed in looksmaxxing culture as a hardmaxxing procedure, it repositions the whole upper jaw to treat long-face problems and under-grown upper jaws. The change in facial structure is visible. The surgical literature is solid but has little on looks outcomes.

summary: Whole upper jaw cut and repositioned (Le Fort I) for long-face problems; a major, established jaw operation with solid surgical literature but little on looks outcomes.
note: Major surgery under general anaesthesia; risks include infection, nerve numbness and bleeding.
currentQuick:
Total maxillary osteotomy moves the entire upper jaw, usually by a Le Fort I cut, to a new position. Medically it treats long face (vertical maxillary excess), open bite and under-grown upper jaws.
In looksmaxxing it is a hardmaxx option for changing facial proportions. Published work is mainly about surgical technique, healing and blood supply; no study in the reviewed material measures attractiveness outcomes.
How it works: Surgeons cut the maxilla horizontally, free it from the skull base, move it forward, up or down, and fix it, usually coordinated with orthodontic braces. Blood supply is preserved through the palatal soft tissue attached to the segment [3].
Risks and caveats: General references list bleeding, swelling, infection, nausea, and facial numbness that is usually temporary but can be permanent. Healing takes weeks, with months for bone remodelling, and it is a major operation requiring general or sedated care.
deepLead:
Total maxillary osteotomy, usually performed as a Le Fort I osteotomy, is an orthognathic (jaw) operation in which the whole upper jaw is cut free from the skull base and moved to a new position, then fixed in place. In the medical literature it is used for conditions such as vertical maxillary excess (often called long face syndrome), open bite and under-grown upper jaws, for example in cleft lip and palate . In looksmaxxing culture it is classed as a hardmaxxing procedure, meaning a bone-level surgical change to facial structure.
Published research on the operation is mostly surgical: animal and cadaver studies of how the upper jaw keeps its blood supply after being cut, cephalometric (X-ray measurement) studies of skeletal change, and studies of related effects such as middle-ear function . Registered trials focus on peri-operative questions such as anaesthesia, bleeding and pain control rather than on facial appearance outcomes .
Risks described in general references include bleeding, swelling, infection, nerve numbness and, rarely, permanent nerve injury; recovery involves weeks of healing and months of bone remodelling . This is a major operation normally planned by surgeons together with orthodontists.

name: Medpor chin implant

chain: Porous implant placed on chin bone
angle.text: Used to add chin projection and balance a recessed profile, with tissue growing into the porous material to anchor it. The added projection is visible. It is an established option with little comparative trial data.

summary: Hard porous polyethylene chin implant that tissue grows into; established chin option with little comparative trial data.
note: Tissue ingrowth makes removal harder than with smooth implants.
currentQuick:
Medpor is a high-density porous polyethylene used for chin implants. It is one of the three common synthetic chin materials, alongside silicone and ePTFE.
It is discussed in looksmaxxing as a hardmaxx way to add chin projection. Published evidence in the reviewed material is thin, mostly technique descriptions.
How it works: A shaped implant is placed over the chin bone; tissue grows into its pores, anchoring it and supporting blood supply [1].
Risks and caveats: General risks of chin implants include swelling, hematoma, temporary numbness, infection, displacement and nerve damage. Porous implants are described as harder to remove because tissue grows into them.
deepLead:
A Medpor chin implant is a chin augmentation implant made of high-density porous polyethylene, a hard, porous and slightly flexible material. Tissue grows into its pores, which anchors it and supports blood supply, but also makes it harder to remove than non-porous alternatives . It is one of several alloplastic (synthetic) options alongside silicone and expanded PTFE .
In looksmaxxing it is categorised as a hardmaxxing option for chin projection. Published material on it is limited; one plastic-surgery paper describes a modified technique for Asian patients, in which the outer aspect of the implant is reshaped to create an appropriate chin shape .

name: ePTFE (Gore-Tex) facial implant

chain: Added chin, lip or nose volume
angle.text: A Gore-Tex-type implant used to add volume to the chin, lips, nasolabial folds and nose. The added contour is visible once healed. Cosmetic studies are small and mostly older.

summary: Gore-Tex-type porous synthetic implant used for chin, lip, nasolabial and nasal augmentation; cosmetic studies are small and mostly older.
note: Porous material that tissue grows into; cosmetic evidence limited to small series and reviews.
currentQuick:
Expanded PTFE, sold as Gore-Tex, is a flexible porous synthetic used in implants for the chin, lips, nasolabial folds and nose. It was developed in 1969 and is widely used elsewhere in medicine, for example in grafts and sutures.
Cosmetic evidence in the reviewed material is limited to a lip-augmentation study, a rhinoplasty literature review and an Asian nasal dorsum study.
How it works: The microporous material is shaped and placed in a pocket, in the chin attached to bone with titanium screws, and tissue grows into its pores to help hold it [2].
Risks and caveats: General implant risks include swelling, infection, displacement and nerve injury. Surgeons quoted in the rhinoplasty review express hesitation about alloplast use because of historical experience with earlier nasal implants [4].
deepLead:
Expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE), best known under the brand name Gore-Tex, is a flexible, porous synthetic material used in facial implants for the chin, lips, nasolabial folds and nose, as well as in many non-cosmetic medical devices. Expanded PTFE was produced in 1969 by Robert Gore, who rapidly stretched heated PTFE to create a microporous structure; because it is nearly inert in the body and allows tissue to grow into it, it is used in vascular grafts, sutures, heart patches and other implants .
In chin augmentation, ePTFE is described as flexible, strong and porous, fixed to bone with titanium screws, with tissue ingrowth providing most of the hold . Published cosmetic studies in the reviewed material are limited: a 1997 evaluation of Gore-Tex lip augmentation , a literature review of ePTFE in rhinoplasty that notes both advocates and opponents of alloplast use , and a comparison study in Asian nasal dorsal augmentation .

name: Silicone chin implant

chain: Soft implant placed on chin bone
angle.text: One of the most common ways to add chin projection, using a soft implant that can be removed easily. The profile change is visible straight away. Published evidence is mostly on complications.

summary: Soft, removable synthetic implant for chin projection; common option, with published evidence mostly on complications.
note: Can shift, buckle, resorb bone or become infected, sometimes years later.
currentQuick:
A silicone chin implant is a shaped piece of silicone placed over the chin bone to add projection. It is among the most common chin implant materials and is relatively easy to remove.
In looksmaxxing it is one of the standard hardmaxx chin options, discussed alongside Medpor and sliding genioplasty.
How it works: The implant sits in a pocket and does not bond to tissue, so its position depends on the pocket being accurately made [1].
Risks and caveats: Reported issues include movement, buckling, bone resorption, infection (including late infection) and soft tissue deformity [1][2][3].
deepLead:
A silicone chin implant is a solid, shaped alloplastic implant placed in front of the chin bone to increase projection. A general reference describes silicone as among the most commonly used chin implant materials: soft and flexible, but not bonding to tissue, so the pocket must be made precisely, with risks of movement, buckling or bone resorption; it can be removed easily .
In looksmaxxing it is classed as a hardmaxx option and is often compared with porous polyethylene (Medpor), ePTFE and bone-cutting sliding genioplasty . Published material in the reviewed sources consists of case reports and surgeon series on complications and on facial augmentation.

name: Mersiline mesh implant

chain: Chin or facial area built up
angle.text: Named in a chin-augmentation reference as an alternative implant material, apparently corresponding to Mersilene polyester mesh. Its facial-augmentation use is mentioned only in passing, and cosmetic data are essentially absent.

summary: Polyester mesh named as a facial-augmentation material, but backed by essentially no cosmetic data.
note: Cosmetic use is poorly documented; established uses are in hernia, prolapse and eyelid surgery.
currentQuick:
Mersiline is listed as a mesh scaffold among alternative chin implant materials. It seems to refer to Mersilene, a polyester mesh long used in hernia and other surgery.
In looksmaxxing it is a niche hardmaxx implant option; no cosmetic studies were found.
How it works: A woven synthetic mesh is placed as a scaffold in the tissue. Its established uses are as reinforcement or suspension material elsewhere in the body [2][4].
Risks and caveats: Cosmetic risks are not documented in the reviewed sources. Studies of Mersilene mesh in other body regions report complications, for example in ptosis surgery [4].
deepLead:
Mersiline mesh is named in a general reference on chin augmentation as one of several alternative implant materials, described there as a mesh scaffold, alongside acellular dermal matrix and braided suture material (Supramid) . The name appears to correspond to Mersilene, a Dacron (polyester) surgical mesh used for decades in hernia repair, prolapse surgery and eyelid-lifting (frontalis suspension) procedures .
Evidence on its use for facial augmentation is very thin. The reviewed medical literature on Mersilene mesh concerns non-cosmetic uses, and a review of alloplastic materials in rhinoplasty is the closest facial-surgery reference . In looksmaxxing it is listed as a hardmaxx implant option for facial contouring, but no cosmetic study of it was found in the material reviewed.

name: Mustardé otoplasty

angle.text: A long-established ear-pinning technique used to set back prominent ears by creating a fold with stitches, without cutting cartilage. The pinned-back ear is visible once healed. Support is mostly retrospective series.

summary: Mattress-suture ear pinning that builds the antihelical fold; a long-established technique backed mostly by retrospective series.
note: Suture extrusion, hematoma, infection and overcorrection are documented complications.
currentQuick:
The Mustardé technique sets back prominent ears by placing permanent mattress sutures that create the antihelical fold, without cutting through the cartilage. It dates to a 1963 paper by J. C. Mustardé.
It is a standard ear procedure; published evidence is mostly retrospective series and technique descriptions.
How it works: The back of the ear cartilage is exposed, skin is trimmed, and mattress sutures fold the antihelix, which pulls the rim closer to the head [1].
Risks and caveats: Documented complications include hematoma, infection, suture extrusion with granulomas, scarring and overcorrection or unnatural contour [1][8].
deepLead:
Mustardé otoplasty is a technique for correcting prominent ears in which permanent mattress sutures are placed to create or deepen the antihelical fold, setting back the helical rim without cutting the cartilage. It is based on J. C. Mustardé's 1963 paper on correcting prominent ears with simple mattress sutures . A general reference classes it among techniques that keep the ear cartilage intact, describing it as an open method in which the cartilage at the back of the ear is exposed, a strip of skin removed and mattress sutures placed .
It is described as commonly used for prominent ear deformity . A retrospective study of patients under 18 characterised it as a "good-fast-cheap" technique when assessed for quality, time and cost . In looksmaxxing it is categorised as a hardmaxx ear procedure; community material was not part of the sources reviewed.

name: Furnas suture technique

chain: Stitches link ear bowl to mastoid
angle.text: An ear-pinning method for ears that stick out because of a deep bowl, often paired with the Mustardé technique. The set-back ear is visible after healing. Evidence is case series, with a known recurrence risk.

summary: Concha-to-mastoid stitches that pin back a deep ear bowl; an established surgical technique with case-series evidence and a known recurrence risk.
note: Suture extrusion and recurrence are reported; surgeon-performed only.
currentQuick:
The Furnas technique is an ear-pinning method that sutures the concha to the bone-covering tissue behind the ear to bring a protruding ear closer to the head. It leaves the cartilage uncut and is often combined with Mustardé sutures.
It is a long-established otoplasty approach documented in surgical case series, mainly for prominent ears in children and adults.
How it works: Stitches anchor the back of the conchal bowl to the mastoid periosteum, reducing the ear-to-head angle without cutting cartilage.
Risks and caveats: Reported complications include hematoma, infection, suture extrusion, overcorrection and recurrence from suture fatigue or cartilage memory. Surgeons have described flaps to reduce extrusion and recurrence.
deepLead:
The Furnas suture technique is an otoplasty (ear surgery) method that sets back a prominent ear by placing permanent or long-lasting sutures between the conchal cartilage (the bowl of the ear) and the mastoid periosteum behind the ear. It was described by David Furnas in 1968 and is often paired with the Mustardé technique, which forms the antihelical fold with mattress sutures.
It addresses ears whose prominence comes mainly from a deep or wide concha. Because it leaves the cartilage uncut, it belongs to the group of cartilage-sparing otoplasty methods. In looksmaxxing discussions it is classed as a surgical (hardmaxx) option for the ears.
Published work consists of surgical technique papers and case series. A 2025 overview describes the preparation, surgical steps, postoperative care and complications of Mustardé and Furnas otoplasty, and other surgeons report that these suture methods can recur because of cartilage memory and suture fatigue.

name: Stenström technique

angle.text: An ear-pinning procedure that scores the front of the cartilage so it folds back, used to correct prominent ears. The pinned result is visible once healed. It has been used surgically for decades and is supported by case series.

summary: Ear pinning by scoring the front of the antihelix cartilage so it folds; long used surgically, supported by case series.
note: Surgeon-performed; overcorrection, hematoma and recurrence are reported.
currentQuick:
The Stenström technique shapes a prominent ear by scoring or rasping the front of the cartilage so it bends back into a natural fold. It dates to 1963 and remains in use, especially in France.
Published results are surgical case series reporting high correction and satisfaction rates.
How it works: Abrading the antihelical cartilage weakens one side so the cartilage curves toward the intact side, recreating the missing fold.
Risks and caveats: General otoplasty complications include hematoma, infection, suture extrusion, asymmetry and overcorrection. Controlled trials are not available.
deepLead:
The Stenström technique (Stenström otoplasty) is an ear-pinning procedure in which the front surface of the antihelical cartilage is scored or rasped so that the cartilage bends backward and forms a fold. It was described by Sten Stenström in 1963.
It is used for prominent ears caused by a failure of the antihelix to fold. Wikipedia describes the principle as weakening the cartilage on one side so it curves toward the intact side. Surgeons in France are reported to use it widely, and modified versions are published.
Evidence consists of surgical series and technique papers; published satisfaction and effectiveness figures come from case series, not controlled trials.

name: Merck stitch otoplasty

angle.text: A closed, minimally invasive ear-pinning method that reshapes the ear using stitches placed through tiny incisions. The pinned-back ear is visible after healing. It is documented, with little published outcome data.

summary: A closed ear-pinning method using stitches through tiny stab incisions; documented but with little published outcome data.
note: Few published outcome data located.
currentQuick:
The Merck stitch is a closed ear-pinning technique placing sutures through small puncture incisions instead of an open posterior incision. It was published in 2013.
Sources describing it are sparse.
How it works: Sutures placed through stab incisions reshape the cartilage without cutting it.
Risks and caveats: General suture-otoplasty risks include suture extrusion, hematoma, infection and recurrence; no technique-specific studies were found.
deepLead:
The Merck stitch is a closed, minimally invasive otoplasty method in which sutures are placed through small stab incisions to reshape the ear without cutting the cartilage. Wikipedia dates its publication to 2013.
It falls within the suture-only (cartilage-intact) group of otoplasty techniques and is contrasted with Mustardé's open approach, which uses a larger incision. Published sources reviewed here give limited detail, and no clinical studies were found.

name: Incisionless Fritsch otoplasty

angle.text: An ear-pinning approach that avoids a skin incision by placing stitches with needles, sometimes with light scoring of cartilage. The reshaped ear is visible after healing. It is documented in publications from 1995 to 2009, with thin outcome data.

summary: Ear pinning with needle-placed stitches through the skin and no incision; documented, but outcome data are thin.
note: Described as suited to milder cases; few outcome data located.
currentQuick:
Incisionless otoplasty reshapes the ear using sutures passed through the skin by needle, avoiding a cut behind the ear. Fritsch published on it between 1995 and 2009.
Sources are brief.
How it works: Percutaneous sutures fold the antihelix and set back the concha, sometimes with scoring.
Risks and caveats: No technique-specific studies were found; general otoplasty risks apply, and sources describe it as suited to mild to moderate prominence.
deepLead:
Incisionless (percutaneous) otoplasty, associated with Fritsch, places sutures through the skin with needles to shape the antihelix and conchal bowl, without a skin incision. Wikipedia dates Fritsch's publications on the method from 1995 to 2009 and notes it may be combined with superficial scoring of the cartilage.
Grokipedia describes incisionless suturing generally as suited to mild to moderate prominent ears, without naming a technique. No clinical studies were found for this specific method in the sources reviewed.

name: Converse–Wood-Smith otoplasty

angle.text: An older cartilage-cutting ear-pinning method that builds a natural-looking fold for prominent ears. The corrected ear shape is visible after healing. Little modern human data has been located.

summary: A cartilage-cutting ear-pinning method using parallel full-thickness incisions to build a fold; older, with little modern human data located.
note: Cartilage-cutting methods are described as carrying higher hematoma and deformity risk.
currentQuick:
This otoplasty cuts through ear cartilage in parallel lines and uses tubing sutures so the cartilage forms an antihelical fold. It stems from Converse's 1955 work.
Only animal research and general descriptions were found.
How it works: Full-thickness cartilage incisions let it bend into a fold held by sutures.
Risks and caveats: Surgeons report hematoma, skin necrosis and ear deformity concerns with cartilage-cutting methods, which contributed to a shift toward suture-only techniques.
deepLead:
The Converse–Wood-Smith technique forms an antihelix by making full-thickness incisions through the ear cartilage and shaping it with tubing sutures. Wikipedia describes it as two parallel cartilage incisions with sutures that create a more natural fold; Converse described a cartilage-incision method in 1955.
It belongs to the cartilage-cutting group of otoplasty methods. Surgeons have noted that cartilage-cutting techniques carry risks of hematoma, skin necrosis and ear deformity, which led to growing use of suture-based methods.

name: Earlobe reduction/repair

angle.text: A minor procedure used to mend torn or split earlobes from heavy earrings or gauges, or to shrink oversized lobes. The tidier lobe is visible once healed. The literature is many technique papers and small case series.

summary: Minor plastic surgery to mend torn or split earlobes or reduce large ones; many technique papers, small case series.
note: Notching of the lobe edge is the outcome technique papers aim to avoid.
currentQuick:
Earlobe repair mends torn or split lobes, often from heavy earrings or stretched piercings; reduction shrinks or repositions large lobes.
The literature is mostly small technique series.
How it works: Surgeons excise scar or excess tissue and close with Z-plasty, L-plasty, V-flap or double-flap designs to prevent notching.
Risks and caveats: Reported issues include notching at the lobe rim; one L-plasty series reported no complications. Larger controlled studies were not found.
deepLead:
Earlobe repair and reduction are surgical procedures that reshape or mend the earlobe. Repair addresses torn or split lobes, often from heavy earrings, trauma or gauged piercings, while reduction addresses oversized or protruding lobes.
Published sources are mostly surgical technique papers describing Z-plasty, L-plasty, V-flap and double-flap closures intended to avoid notching of the lobe edge. A paper on cosmetic repair notes that piercing-related complications are rising with the popularity of body piercing.

name: Ear cartilage molding (EarWell)

angle.text: A non-surgical splint system for newborns with prominent, cup or lop ears, reshaping soft infant cartilage over several weeks. Studies report high correction rates when started in the first weeks. It is a newborn option and not used for adults.

summary: A newborn-only splint system that reshapes soft infant ear cartilage; studies report high correction rates when started in the first weeks, and it is not an adult option.
note: Published studies describe a narrow window: results are reported to be best when started in the first days to weeks of life, and some ears relapse.
currentQuick:
Ear molding is a non-surgical treatment for babies born with ear shape differences such as prominent (cup or protruding) ears, lop ears, Stahl's ear or constricted ears. A small molded device and adhesive are applied to the ear for a period of weeks to guide the cartilage into a more typical shape. The EarWell Infant Ear Correction System is one commercial version.
It appears in looksmaxxing discussions because ear shape is sometimes raised as a facial feature, and molding is cited as an example of a correction that works only very early in life. Published studies are mostly single-centre case series rather than randomised trials, and they report high success rates when treatment starts early.
How it works: Researchers attribute the effect to maternal estrogen still circulating in the newborn, which keeps ear cartilage unusually pliable for the first weeks of life. A molding device holds the folds of the ear (antihelix, helical rim, conchal area) in a corrected position while the cartilage sets.
Risks and caveats: Reported complications in the studies are mostly skin irritation, pressure sores and abrasions; one tropical-climate series reported skin complications in 46 percent of infants. Some ears relapse after treatment, and severe constricted ears respond less well. Studies report that results decline when treatment starts after the first weeks of life.
deepLead:
Ear molding, also called infant ear splinting or newborn ear correction, is a non-surgical treatment for congenital ear deformities in which a small device is attached to a baby's ear for several weeks to reshape the cartilage. Conditions treated include prominent or cup ears, lop (lidding) ears, Stahl's ear, helical rim abnormalities, cryptotia and constricted ears . The EarWell Infant Ear Correction System is a commercial product built around this method .
Authors of the main clinical series say the technique relies on the plasticity of newborn ear cartilage, which they attribute to maternal estrogen circulating in the infant during the first weeks of life . In one single-physician review of 488 patients, only about 30 percent of congenital ear deformities were reported to self-correct .
Evidence consists of retrospective and prospective case series, with success rates in the mid-80 to mid-90 percent range reported in different cohorts, and most authors reporting better results when molding starts in the first one to two weeks . No randomised trial results were found among the published studies reviewed; one randomised comparison of two molding protocols is registered as recruiting . In looksmaxxing communities the topic appears mainly as a reference point for what can and cannot be changed about ear shape after infancy.

name: Corner lip lift

angle.text: Used to lift downturned mouth corners, widen the mouth and make lips look fuller, often with an upper lip lift. The new mouth angle is visible. Evidence is surgeon case experience, and some surgeons advise against it to protect white lip length.

summary: Surgical skin excision at the corners of the mouth to raise downturned commissures; evidence is surgeon case experience, and visible scarring is a recognised risk.
note: Scarring at the mouth corner, asymmetry and under-correction are documented risks; published evidence is mostly surgeon series.
currentQuick:
A corner lip lift is a surgical procedure in which a small piece of skin is removed at or just above the corner of the mouth so that downturned corners sit higher. It is sometimes called a smile lift. It is often performed together with an upper lip lift, and some surgeons describe it as a way to widen the visible lip.
On looksmax.org, users discuss it as a way to change mouth proportions and make lips look fuller or the smile more prominent. Published literature consists mainly of surgeon-authored descriptions and case series; no controlled trials were found.
How it works: Skin is excised in a lens or triangle shape above the oral commissure and the wound is closed, which pulls the corner upward. Some variants also involve the muscles around the mouth. Reports describe the result as a change of a few millimetres.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include visible scarring, hypertrophic scarring, asymmetry, under-correction, stiffness, numbness and distortion of the smile. A surgeon-authored review states that lip lift design is more complex than most practitioners realize. Some posters on looksmax.org say surgeons advised against the procedure for aesthetic reasons.
deepLead:
A corner lip lift (also called corner of the mouth lift, commissure lift or smile lift) is a surgical procedure that raises the corners of the mouth, typically by removing a small, lens-shaped piece of skin at or above the oral commissure . It is performed to alter the resting angle of the mouth in people whose corners turn downward, and is often combined with an upper lip lift .
Plastic surgery literature on the technique is largely descriptive. A 2022 article in the Aesthetic Surgery Journal by authors who reported over 2,440 consecutive lip lifts discusses when to add a corner lift to a deep-plane upper lip lift . Wikipedia notes that surgeons report high satisfaction but that no single lip lift technique has become standard .
Within looksmaxxing communities, the corner lip lift is discussed in terms of mouth width, lip fullness and facial proportions, alongside jaw and chin procedures .

name: Gore-Tex lip implant (SoftForm)

chain: Tube of ePTFE placed in lip
angle.text: A tubular Gore-Tex-type implant placed in the lip for permanent added volume, sold under names like Advanta, UltraSoft and SoftForm. The fuller lip is visible after healing. Sources reviewed describe it only briefly.

summary: A tubular expanded-PTFE implant placed in the lip for permanent volume; the sources reviewed describe it only briefly and report implant movement and extrusion as risks.
note: Sources reviewed contain no clinical studies of this implant; implant movement and extrusion are listed complications of lip implants generally.
currentQuick:
Gore-Tex lip implants are thin strips or tubes of expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE) that a surgeon places in the lip to add permanent volume. Wikipedia lists SoftForm, Advanta and UltraSoft as commercial versions, in diameters of 1.6 mm or 4.8 mm.
The material is a long-established surgical implant in vascular and facial plastic surgery. No clinical studies specific to lip use were found in the sources reviewed, so this entry is short.
How it works: The implant is a solid or hollow ePTFE tube inserted into the lip tissue, where it physically occupies space and so increases lip volume.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia lists implant movement and extrusion (breaking through the tissue) among complications of lip implants, along with bleeding, asymmetry and lumpiness. Unlike hyaluronic acid fillers, an implant is a physical device rather than an injectable.
deepLead:
Gore-Tex lip implants are strips or tubes of expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE) used for lip augmentation. Wikipedia describes them as 1.6 mm or 4.8 mm in diameter and names Advanta, UltraSoft and SoftForm as commercial versions .
ePTFE is also used as a graft and implant material in vascular, cardiac, hernia and facial plastic surgery . For lips specifically, the sources reviewed provide little beyond a description and a list of complications, and no clinical studies were found.

name: Alloderm lip augmentation

angle.text: Uses processed donor skin placed in small rolls in the lip to add size, or along the lip border to sharpen it. The added volume is visible once healed. Sources reviewed give only a short description and one 2000 paper title.

summary: Lip volume from processed donor skin (AlloDerm) placed in rolls in the lip; sources reviewed give only a short description and one 2000 journal paper title.
note: Sources reviewed contain no outcome data for this use.
currentQuick:
AlloDerm is donor skin from cadavers that has been processed to remove living cells. In lip augmentation, surgeons have placed it in small rolls in the lip or along the border of the lip to add size or sharpen the edge, according to Wikipedia.
A 2000 paper in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery is titled "Alloderm lip augmentation", but its abstract was not available, and no outcome data were found in the sources reviewed.
How it works: Rolled or layered donor dermal tissue is inserted into the lip mucosa to add bulk, or into the vermilion border to define it.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed give no specific complication data for this use. Wikipedia lists general lip augmentation complications such as swelling, bruising, asymmetry and lumpiness.
deepLead:
AlloDerm lip augmentation uses processed donor (cadaver) dermis to add volume to the lips. Wikipedia says it is placed in small rolls in the mucosa to add size, or in the vermilion to sharpen the lip border .
A paper titled "Alloderm lip augmentation" appeared in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery in 2000 . Beyond that, no outcome data were found in the sources reviewed.

name: Dermalogen / Autologen

angle.text: Injectable fillers made from human collagen, from the patient's own skin (Autologen) or donor tissue (Dermalogen), used to add volume to lips and soften lines. The filling is visible after injection. Sources describe short-to-moderate persistence.

summary: Collagen injectables made from skin (the patient's own for Autologen, donor for Dermalogen); sources describe them as dermal fillers with short-to-moderate persistence and no allergy testing needed.
note: Evidence is limited to an early-2000s review and descriptions; results are described as temporary.
currentQuick:
Autologen and Dermalogen are injectable fillers made from human dermal collagen. Autologen is processed from the patient's own skin; Dermalogen is made from donor tissue. A 2000 article on facial soft-tissue augmentation described them as physiologic and consistent with many qualities of an ideal dermal filler.
Wikipedia says Autologen carries no allergy risk but is absorbed quickly, so results are very temporary, and that some studies suggest Dermalogen lasts somewhat longer than standard collagen. A 2004 review classed them as autograft and homograft fillers respectively.
How it works: Human collagen is processed and injected into the skin, where it adds volume until the body gradually absorbs it.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed describe low immune risk because the material is human-derived, and temporary results. No detailed safety trials were found.
deepLead:
Autologen and Dermalogen are injectable dermal fillers consisting of human tissue collagen matrix. Autologen is derived from the patient's own skin, and Dermalogen from donor (allogeneic) tissue .
A 2000 article in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery described dermal augmentation with these matrices as physiologic and as appearing ultimately safe and effective, with many qualities of an ideal filler . A 2004 review of injectables placed Autologen among autografts and Dermalogen among homografts, noting that no perfect filler exists .
Wikipedia's lip augmentation article says Autologen has no allergy risk but is absorbed rapidly, and that Dermalogen may last slightly longer than standard collagen, though that claim is marked as needing a citation .

name: Mucomuscular flap lip augmentation

angle.text: A surgical lip enlargement that moves tissue from inside the mouth into the lip for more size. The change is visible once healed. The only source reviewed describes flaps generally as adding little volume and slight protrusion.

summary: Surgical lip enlargement by moving intraoral tissue into the lip; the only source reviewed describes flaps generally as adding little volume.
note: Very thin sourcing: no studies specific to this technique were found.
currentQuick:
Surgical flap procedures move small strips of tissue from near the lips or inside the mouth into the lip. Wikipedia says this adds little volume and gives only slight protrusion.
No studies specific to mucomuscular flap augmentation were found, and the registered trials surfaced under this name concern dental implants and bone grafting.
How it works: A strip of mucosa and underlying muscle is repositioned within the lip to increase bulk.
Risks and caveats: General lip surgery risks listed on Wikipedia include bleeding, swelling, uneven lips and lumpiness; no figures for this technique were found.
deepLead:
Mucomuscular flap lip augmentation refers to surgical lip enlargement using tissue from inside the mouth. Wikipedia describes lip augmentation by flaps, in which small strips of skin from near the lips or inside the mouth are moved to the lips, and says this adds little volume and produces only slight protrusion .
No clinical studies specific to this technique were found, so this entry is brief.

name: Lip plumper (capsaicin)

angle.text: A chili-based lip gloss, sometimes with menthol or cinnamon, used as a non-injectable way to make lips look fuller for a short time. The swelling is visible within minutes. The volume is brief and formal evidence is thin.

summary: A chili-based lip gloss that irritates the lips into swelling for a short while; the volume is brief and the evidence thin.
note: Irritant reactions and contact allergy to lip cosmetics are documented.
currentQuick:
Capsaicin lip plumpers are glosses or balms that contain a chili-derived irritant, sometimes alongside menthol, cinnamon or ginger. They produce a tingle or burn and a short-lived swelling that makes lips look fuller.
Products are positioned as a needle-free alternative to filler. Published evidence is limited to small, mostly open-label studies of branded products.
How it works: Capsaicin activates heat-sensitive receptors on sensory nerves and is described as increasing blood flow and causing mild swelling. The effect is reported to last from minutes to a few hours.
Risks and caveats: Case reports and reviews document contact urticaria and allergic contact reactions to lip cosmetics. Grokipedia reports that frequent use of irritant formulas may cause dryness and sensitivity.
deepLead:
A capsaicin lip plumper is a topical cosmetic applied to the lips that uses an irritant, most often capsaicin from chili peppers, sometimes with menthol, cinnamon, peppermint or ginger, to produce a brief tingling or burning sensation and temporary swelling that makes the lips look fuller. It is marketed as a non-injectable alternative to lip filler.
Irritant formulas are described as working by stimulating nerve endings and increasing local blood flow, with effects reported to last from minutes to a few hours. A separate class of "hydration-based" plumpers relies on humectants such as hyaluronic acid and does not aim to irritate.
Published evidence is limited to small, mostly open-label studies of proprietary products, many of which combine several ingredients. Case reports and reviews document contact urticaria and allergic contact reactions to lip cosmetics, including plumpers.
